sentences.text: Probrachylophosaurus was a large, four-legged herbivore about 10 meters long with a large beak and slender front limbs paired with strong hind limbs.
This dinosaur possessed a wide, backward-projecting head crest supported by long striations along the frontal and nasal bones.
In Probrachylophosaurus, the frontals covering the nasal attachment area cover only about 59% of the frontal bone, compared to full coverage in adult Brachylophosaurus.
The holotype specimen of Probrachylophosaurus is the largest known member of the brachysaurolophine group and was nicknamed "Super-Duck" due to its massive size.
A specific specimen of Probrachylophosaurus reached an age of fourteen years when it died, making it one of the oldest known individuals of its kind.
The display crest on the head of Probrachylophosaurus grew significantly later in life than the rest of the skeleton.
The genus Probrachylophosaurus was described by Freedman Fowler and Horner in 2015.
The first fossils of Probrachylophosaurus were discovered in Montana in 1981, but the skeleton was not fully excavated until 2008.
The specific name 'bergei' honors Sam Berge, a landowner who supported the research.
Fossilized gut contents indicate that Probrachylophosaurus ate leaves, consistent with other hadrosaurs.
Sexual maturity in Probrachylophosaurus appears to have been reached at approximately five years of age.
A fourteen-year-old Probrachylophosaurus specimen had reached 95% of its maximum size by the age of nine.
Studies indicate Probrachylophosaurus had a maximum growth rate of 855 kg per year between the ages of 3.64 and 4.64 years.
Histologic analysis indicates that Probrachylophosaurus experienced fast growth rates similar to other hadrosaurs.
Comparisons with Maiasaura suggest Probrachylophosaurus took approximately twice as long to reach sexual maturity.
The left tibia showed fourteen lines of arrested growth, which likely represent annual seasons of poor food consumption, suggesting the holotype was around fourteen years old.
The lower jaw of the Probrachylophosaurus type specimen shows three circular depressions surrounded by raised bone rings.
Six vertebrae in the middle of the tail of the Probrachylophosaurus type specimen show healed breakage across their neural spines.
Recent research suggests that mating behavior, specifically mounting by males, is the most likely cause of the healed tail injuries found in Probrachylophosaurus.
Evidence of injuries, including fractured tail vertebrae, suggests Probrachylophosaurus may have interacted aggressively with other hadrosaurs.
Probrachylophosaurus is a solid-crested hadrosaur belonging to the subfamily Saurolophinae and the tribe Brachylophosaurini.
Probrachylophosaurus is thought to be a close relative of Brachylophosaurus and Ornatops and a possible descendant of Acristavus.
Fossils of Probrachylophosaurus date to the Campanian age between 80.45 and 79 million years ago.
The discovery of Probrachylophosaurus suggests that brachylophosaurs were among the first hadrosaurs to colonize fluvial lowlands after the Claggett Seaway receded.
It is debated whether the specimen Brachylophosaurus goodwini is a distinct species or merely a younger specimen of Probrachylophosaurus bergei.
Early phylogenetic analyses disagreed on whether Probrachylophosaurus was a close relative of Brachylophosaurus or a sister taxon to a group containing both Brachylophosaurus and Maiasaura.
Scientists have proposed multiple causes for tail injuries in hadrosaurs, including predator attacks, herd trampling, biomechanical stress, and mating behavior.
